subject: combined-science

items.q: In diffusion, the particles of a substance in solution show a net movement:
items.correct: from a higher to a lower concentration, without energy
items.misconception: from a lower to a higher concentration, requiring energy from respiration
items.why: Both processes are described as getting substances into cells, so students focus on the destination rather than on the concentrations on each side of the membrane. Diffusion results in a net movement from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration. Active transport moves substances from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated solution, against a concentration gradient, and this requires energy from respiration.
items.random_wrong: from a lower to a higher concentration, using no energy

items.q: The concentration of oxygen in the air inside the alveoli is raised. Everything else, including the temperature, stays the same. What happens to the rate of diffusion of oxygen into the blood?
items.correct: It rises, as the concentration gradient is steeper
items.misconception: It falls, as a steeper gradient crowds particles
items.why: Students picture a crowd of particles as blocked rather than as more likely to spread outwards, and everyday experience of crowds slowing movement supports the idea. The difference in concentrations (concentration gradient) is one of the factors which affect the rate of diffusion: the greater the difference in concentrations, the faster the rate of diffusion.
items.random_wrong: It stays the same, as the temperature has not risen

items.q: Cube A has sides 1 mm long. Cube B has sides 2 mm long. Which statement about their surface area to volume ratios is correct?
items.correct: Cube A has a ratio of 6:1 and cube B a ratio of 3:1
items.misconception: Cube A has a ratio of 3:1 and cube B one of 6:1
items.why: Students compare surface areas instead of ratios. Because a large organism obviously has more surface, they conclude that the ratio must be larger too. Volume increases faster than surface area, so the surface area to volume ratio falls as size increases. A single-celled organism has a relatively large surface area to volume ratio, which allows sufficient transport of molecules into and out of the cell to meet the needs of the organism.
items.random_wrong: Cube A has a ratio of 3:1 and cube B one of 12:1

items.q: Why do large multicellular organisms need specialised exchange surfaces and a transport system?
items.correct: Their surface area to volume ratio is too small for diffusion
items.misconception: Their surface area to volume ratio is too high for diffusion
items.why: Students compare surface areas instead of ratios. Because a large organism obviously has more surface, they conclude that the ratio must be larger too. Volume increases faster than surface area, so the surface area to volume ratio falls as size increases. A single-celled organism has a relatively large surface area to volume ratio, which allows sufficient transport of molecules into and out of the cell to meet the needs of the organism.
items.random_wrong: Their surface area to volume ratio increases as they get bigger

items.q: Which feature of the alveoli in the lungs increases the effectiveness of gas exchange?
items.correct: A thin wall that provides a short diffusion path
items.misconception: A thick wall holding the gases in for longer
items.why: Students think of absorption as soaking up and storing, so a thick, compact surface seems better than one that is thin and spread out. The effectiveness of an exchange surface is increased by: having a large surface area; a membrane that is thin, to provide a short diffusion path; (in animals) having an efficient blood supply; (in animals, for gaseous exchange) being ventilated.
items.random_wrong: A small surface area that packs cells in

items.q: Osmosis takes place through a partially permeable membrane. Which statement describes it correctly?
items.correct: Water moves from a dilute to a concentrated solution
items.misconception: Water moves from a concentrated solution to a dilute one
items.why: Students correctly remember that diffusion goes from higher to lower concentration, but apply it to the solute they can see rather than to the water molecules that actually cross the membrane. Osmosis is the diffusion of water from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane. The dilute solution is the one with the higher concentration of water.
items.random_wrong: Sugar moves from a dilute solution into a concentrated one

items.q: A potato cylinder has a mass of 4.0 g at the start. After 30 minutes in a sugar solution its mass is 3.4 g. What is the percentage loss of mass, and how is it found?
items.correct: 15.0%, dividing the change by the starting mass
items.misconception: 17.6%, dividing the change by the final mass
items.why: Students use the mass they measured last as the reference value, and percentages are often first met as a part of a total rather than as a change from a starting value. Percentage gain or loss of mass of plant tissue = (change in mass divided by the starting mass) multiplied by 100. The starting mass is the value that the change is divided by.
items.random_wrong: 85.0%, dividing the final mass by the start mass

items.q: A student plots percentage change in mass of potato cylinders on the y-axis against concentration of sugar solution on the x-axis. The line crosses the x-axis, at zero percentage change in mass, at 0.30 mol/dm3. What does this point show?
items.correct: The cells and the solution had equal concentrations
items.misconception: Water moved into the cells from the sugar solution
items.why: Students correctly remember that diffusion goes from higher to lower concentration, but apply it to the solute they can see rather than to the water molecules that actually cross the membrane. Osmosis is the diffusion of water from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane. The dilute solution is the one with the higher concentration of water.
items.random_wrong: The sugar moved out of the cells into the sugar solution

items.q: Root hair cells take up mineral ions from a very dilute solution in the soil. How are the mineral ions taken up?
items.correct: By active transport, which uses energy from respiration
items.misconception: By diffusion, moving down the concentration gradient
items.why: Diffusion is met first and is the process students reach for by default, so they assume a substance entering a cell must be more concentrated outside without checking the actual concentrations. Active transport allows mineral ions to be absorbed into plant root hairs from very dilute solutions in the soil, and sugar molecules to be absorbed from lower concentrations in the gut into the blood which has a higher sugar concentration. Both are movements against a concentration gradient and require energy from respiration.
items.random_wrong: By osmosis, across the partially permeable membrane

items.q: Does diffusion need energy from respiration?
items.correct: No. Diffusion is a net movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration and needs no energy from respiration.
items.misconception: Diffusion, like active transport, uses energy from respiration to move particles across the cell membrane.
items.why: The three transport processes are taught together, and students treat any movement of particles as something that has to be powered, so they attach the energy requirement of active transport to diffusion as well. Diffusion is the spreading out of the particles of any substance in solution, or particles of a gas, resulting in a net movement from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration. Only active transport, which moves substances against a concentration gradient, requires energy from respiration.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What moves through the partially permeable membrane during osmosis?
items.misconception: Dissolved solutes such as sugar cross the membrane along with the water during osmosis.
items.why: Osmosis is introduced as a type of diffusion, so students assume any dissolved particle can cross, and diagrams showing solute particles on both sides of the membrane reinforce the idea. Osmosis is the diffusion of water from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane. It is the water that moves across the membrane.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which factors affect the rate of diffusion?
items.correct: The difference in concentrations, the temperature and the surface area of the membrane.
items.misconception: Temperature is what sets the rate of diffusion, so if the temperature stays the same the rate cannot change.
items.why: Particle theory is usually taught through heating and cooling, so students tie particle movement to temperature alone and overlook the other factors. Factors which affect the rate of diffusion are: the difference in concentrations (concentration gradient); the temperature; the surface area of the membrane. Changing any one of these changes the rate of diffusion.
